(p-6248) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat al-'Asr

Makkan; it is also said to be Madinan. It has three verses.

(p-6249) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:

[1–3] ﴿By the 'Asr (time).﴾ ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss.﴾ [al-'Asr: 2] ﴿Except for those who believe, do righteous deeds, enjoin one another to the truth, and enjoin one another to patience.﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]

﴿By the 'Asr﴾ — that is, time (ad-dahr). The Exalted swore by it because it contains the wonders of affairs, both those that endure and those that pass away. For this reason it has been called "the father of wonder." It is also because it reminds of the blessings within it and their opposites, and so alerts man that he is prepared for both loss and felicity. It is also to honor it and exalt its standing, implying its innocence of the loss and blame that are attributed to it. As it has been said:

People find fault with time, yet there is no fault in it, except for those unworthy of time.

It has also been allowed that by al-'Asr is meant the well-known time in which the 'Asr prayer becomes obligatory.

The Imam (Muhammad 'Abduh) said: It was the custom of the Arabs to gather at the time of 'Asr, converse, and discuss their affairs. Sometimes their talk contained what was unseemly, or what harmed one another. So people would imagine that the time was blameworthy. God therefore swore by it to alert you that time in itself is not something to be blamed and reviled, as people are accustomed to say: "an ill-omened time," "a time of misfortune," "an evil age," and the like. Rather, it counts good deeds just as it counts evil deeds, and it is a vessel for the majestic affairs of God: creation, provision, granting honor and abasement, lowering and raising. So how can it be blamed in itself? What may be blamed is only the detestable deeds that occur within it!

﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2] — that is, in utter loss, because of losing his capital, which is the light of the innate nature (fitra) and the original guidance, by preferring the life of this world and its perishing pleasures, being veiled by them and by time, and squandering the lasting in exchange for the perishing.

﴿Except for those who believe﴾ [al-'Asr: 3] — that is, in God and in what He has sent down of the truth, with a faith that has taken command of their will, (p-6250) so that they do only what accords with their beliefs, as He said: ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]. Al-Qashani said: That is, of virtues and good things; that is, they acquired them, and so they gained an increase of perfecting light over the light of predisposition, which is their capital.

"and enjoin one another to the truth" — that is, they counseled one another to follow what God sent down in His Book of His commands, and to avoid what He forbade of acts of disobedience. ﴿and enjoin one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3] — that is, patience in what God tests His servants with, or patience upon the truth. For arriving at the truth is easy, but remaining upon it and being patient with it through steadfastness and striving for its sake is what reveals the proof and reality of faith.

Points of note:

First: Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in Miftah Dar al-Sa'ada: Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: "If people all reflected on this surah, it would suffice them." The explanation is that there are four levels, and by completing them a person attains the utmost of his perfection:

The first of them: knowledge of the truth. The second: acting upon it.

The third: teaching it to one who does not know it well. The fourth: his patience in learning it, acting upon it and teaching it.

So the Exalted mentioned the four levels in this surah. The Glorified swore by al-'Asr that everyone is in loss, except those who believe, and they are those who knew the truth and affirmed it; this is one level. "and do righteous deeds" — they are those who acted upon what they knew of the truth; this is another. "and enjoin one another to the truth" — they counseled one another with it by way of teaching and guidance; this is a third level. ﴿and enjoin one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3] — they were patient upon the truth and counseled one another to patience in it and to steadfastness; this is a fourth level.

This is the utmost perfection. For perfection is that a person be perfect in himself and perfect others. His perfection lies in setting right his two faculties, the cognitive and the practical. The cognitive faculty is set right by faith, and the practical faculty by doing righteous deeds; and he perfects others by teaching them, by his patience with them, and by counseling them to patience in knowledge and action. Thus this surah, despite its brevity, is among the most comprehensive surahs of the Qur'an for all good, in its entirety. Praise be to God, who made His Book sufficient in place of everything else, a cure for every ailment, and a guide to every good. End of quote.

(p-6251) Second: Al-Razi said: This surah contains a severe warning. For the Exalted ruled that all people are in loss, except whoever brings these four things: faith, righteous deeds, mutual counsel to the truth, and mutual counsel to patience. This shows that salvation depends on all these matters together. And just as the person accountable before God must secure what concerns himself, so too he has duties toward others: among them calling to the religion, giving sincere advice, enjoining the good and forbidding the evil, and loving for him what he loves for himself. Then He repeated the mutual counsel so that the first would include calling to God and the second steadfastness in it; or the first enjoining the good and the second forbidding the evil. Of this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you﴾ [Luqman: 17]. And 'Umar said: "May God have mercy on one who presents me with my faults."

Third: Al-Razi said: The verse shows that the truth is heavy and that trials accompany it; therefore He joined mutual counsel with patience.

Fourth: Singling out mutual counsel to the truth and to patience, though they are included among righteous deeds, is to highlight the perfection of care for them.

The Imam said: Among those deeds are calling to the truth and counseling to patience, but He intended to single out these two by mention, because they are the guardians of every good and the head of every matter. The truth is what is established as a firm reality or a sound law, and it is what a decisive proof, or direct observation and witnessing, guides to. So He made it a condition for salvation from loss that people know the truth, bind themselves to it, give it place in their hearts, and then urge one another to it, each calling his companion to belief in established realities which the intellect does not dispute and in which transmitted knowledge does not differ, and that they keep themselves and others far from the delusions and fancies on which souls have no firm footing and to which no proof guides. That is only by exercising thought and excellent examination of the created universe, until the soul is able to repel the false delusions that come upon it. This frees the intellect from every restriction, while requiring precision in examination, not going along with rashness and being deceived (p-6252) by habit and delusion. Whoever does not take it upon himself to urge people to the sound truth after knowing it is among the losers. See how this is in the verse by the explicit text that admits no reinterpretation.

Patience is a strength of the soul to bear hardship in good work, and to bear the dislike of being deprived of a pleasure, if obtaining it involves something contrary to the truth or what the sound law, in which there is no disagreement, does not permit; and to bear pains when calamities befall, without panic and without overstepping, in repelling them, the bounds of truth and the law. So the condition for salvation from loss is that you be patient, that you counsel others to patience, and urge them to perfect their faculties with this noble virtue, which is the mother of all virtues. You cannot urge him to this until you yourself are adorned with it; otherwise you would enter among those who say and do not do as they say, and would not be among those who do righteous deeds. End of quote.

Fifth: The Imam said: He said ﴿and enjoin one another﴾ [al-'Asr: 3] and did not say "and they enjoined," to show that salvation from loss depends on the eagerness of each individual of the community for the truth, and the inclination of each of them to counsel his people, and whoever is concerned with the matter of truth, so that he counsels his companion to seek it, being concerned that he see the truth and accept it. So in this weighty expression it is as if He explicitly stated their mutual counsel to the truth and their acceptance of the counsel when it is directed to them.

Sixth: Ibn Kathir said: Al-Tabarani mentioned, by way of Hammad ibn Salama, from Thabit, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Hisn, who said: When two men of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) met, they would not part until one of them had recited to the other Surat al-'Asr to its end, and then one of them would greet the other with salam. The Imam said: People have thought that this was for seeking blessing, but that is a mistake. Rather it was so that each of them would remind his companion of what is stated in it, especially the mutual counsel to the truth and to patience, so as to draw out from him before parting any good counsel he might have.

The Imam, may God have mercy on him, interpreted this surah in a separate exegesis for which no like had preceded him; whoever wishes to go deeper into its secrets should refer to it.
